summary:
Before humanity sets foot on Mars, we must test our technology on Earth—without destroying fragile ecosystems in the process. GeoAnalog Space is an interactive Earth–Mars platform built with Python and Folium that transforms NASA open data—MRO (CRISM, HiRISE, MOLA), Mars Odyssey (THEMIS), and Landsat—into an actionable planetary exploration tool. By pairing Parys Mountain in Wales, an extreme acid-mine environment hosting extremophiles, with Mars's ancient Mawrth Vallis and Oyama Crater, our system correlates five key minerals (jarosite, hematite, anglesite, barite, and quartz) to pinpoint ancient liquid water, rover hazards, and high-priority biosignature zones.
To ensure responsible exploration, we introduce an environmental sustainability filter dividing sites into Operational Analogs (disturbed terrains safe for physical rover testing) and Virtual Analogs (protected habitats studied strictly via remote sensing or sterilized, zero-emission microrobots). Looking ahead, we aim to scale GeoAnalog Space into a global, real-time platform integrating live NASA APIs and automated similarity scoring for upcoming Moon and Mars missions.
details:
GeoAnalogSpace It is a platform that serves as a visual and interactive comparison tool, allowing anyone to analyze data comparing terrestrial analog sites—specifically Parys Mountain, Anglesey, Wales (United Kingdom)—with Martian regions, namely Mawrth Vallis, including Oyama and McLaughlin craters. The platform integrates and cross-references open data from five NASA orbital instruments (MRO, HiRISE, CRISM, THEMIS, and MOLA) through layers synchronized by mineralogical composition, black-and-white topography, a Day/Night illumination toggle, scrollable controls, a Zoom Index, and comparative charts for specialists.

It allows teams to validate sensors and assess terrain hazards before deploying rovers or machinery to Mars, reducing operational costs and increasing mission safety while remaining accessible for planetary research.

It was developed using Python (Folium), CSS, and JavaScript, utilizing Google Colab as the processing environment, GitHub for version control, and open NASA datasets on standard laptops.

Instead of displaying tables full of hard-to-read numbers, we turned space exploration into a visual "mirror" between Earth and Mars. Our proposal breaks the barrier between scientific data and anyone's curiosity. We designed an interface where comparing two planets feels as natural as navigating an everyday map, using comparative color codes to connect Parys Mountain with Mawrth Vallis at a glance. We factored in both user visual comfort and practical mission challenges: identifying safe terrain where an exploration vehicle can move without risks.
